assignments.title: 12.7 Primary Source Report: Schenck v. United States and the Limits of Free Speech
assignments.html:
PRIMARY SOURCE REPORT
Schenck v. United States and the Limits of Free Speech
A Supreme Court opinion read alongside the war at sea.
Report · 16 points · Word document upload
✂ ─ ✂ ─ ✂
HOW TO WORK
Read the two lessons and the two primary sources first, and look over your notes in My Notebook. Then write your report in Word and submit it as the submission box below describes.
THE TASK

Write a report of 450 to 650 words in Word. Answer all four questions below, in order, each under its own heading. Use the Schenck excerpt and “Beyond the Western Front: Gallipoli, the Straits, and the U-boats”. Put short quotations in quotation marks and cite each one in a footnote.

You will be graded on the quality of your argument, not on which side you take.

YOUR REPORT

1. Who was Schenck, what did his leaflet say, and what test does Justice Holmes announce? Explain “clear and present danger” and “proximity and degree” in your own words.

2. Holmes writes that “the character of every act depends upon the circumstances in which it is done.” What does he assume about the freedom of a free people when their nation is at war?

3. “Beyond the Western Front: Gallipoli, the Straits, and the U-boats” shows Britain stretching the law of the sea and Germany breaking it, and each pointing to wartime need. Compare that reasoning with Holmes’s reasoning about speech. What is alike, what is different, and is there a point where “necessity” stops being a good reason?

4. Suppose the Court had decided that Schenck’s leaflet was protected by the First Amendment. What might the government, the army, and ordinary citizens have done differently in 1917 and 1918? Say what you think would have been gained or lost, and what you cannot know.

GRADING RUBRIC (16 pts)

SUBMISSION

Write your report in Word and save it to your OneDrive folder. Then open this assignment in Canvas, choose the OneDrive tab, select your file, and submit.

Your teacher will read your report and score it with the rubric above.

MODULE INTRODUCTION
Module Introduction: The People's War
Survey · 3 questions · not graded
✂ ─ ✂ ─ ✂
Before you start

Welcome to The People's War. Answer the questions below before you open the first lesson. Your answers help your teacher see where the class is starting. This survey is not graded.

This module's goals:
  • Describe how governments mobilized whole peoples and used propaganda.
  • Explain how free states limited speech in wartime, and why they said they had to.
  • Follow the three attempts to break the deadlock: the Straits, the blockade, and the U-boats.

discussions.title: 12.8 Discussion: May a free state silence dissent in wartime?
discussions.html:
DISCUSSION
May a free state silence dissent in wartime?
Safety, unity, and the freedom a nation is fighting for.
Graded discussion · 10 points · one post and one reply
✂ ─ ✂ ─ ✂
HOW TO WORK
Read the two lessons and the two primary sources first, and look over your notes in My Notebook. Then post your answer to the prompt below, and reply to one classmate.
DISCUSSION PROMPT

This week’s question: May a free state silence dissent in wartime?

Take a side. Use at least one example from “Mobilizing Whole Peoples: Propaganda and the Home Front”, and say what the state gains and what it risks by the choice you defend.

Write 150 to 250 words. State one claim you believe is true. Then explain why, using the specific evidence named above. Keep to what the lessons and the sources show. If you are guessing, say so.

Then add one sentence on honesty. If a government hides bad news so that its people will keep fighting, does it wrong them, even if it wins? Say what you think and why.

RESPOND TO A CLASSMATE

Reply to one classmate. Do you agree with their reasoning? If so, strengthen it with a fact or decision they did not use. If not, say politely where you think it falls short, and give your reason.

GRADING RUBRIC (10 pts)
CriteriaSubstantive (full credit)Thin (partial credit)Missing (no credit)
Your claim and your reasons
